title: Upgrade wave controller: autoscaler handshake, evacuation budgeting, and pre-warm capacity
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Context:
Redwood Dedicated requires safer, predictable rolling upgrades of GPU pools with minimal customer impact. Existing flocked approaches (per-node drains + ad-hoc autoscaler signals) have led to transient latency spikes and overprovisioning during upgrades. We need a first-class wave controller (upgrade wave manager) that coordinates with autoscaling, respects LTS channel pins, and enforces an evacuation budget at the pool level.

Problem statement:
- Current upgrade flow: drain nodes individually -> rely on cluster autoscaler to replenish -> results in delayed scale-ups or racing scale-downs.
- No formal handshake between upgrade controller and autoscaler: upgrades can cause reactive scale-ups that overshoot or create oscillation.
- Draining GPUs one-by-one causes tail-latency regressions for heavy KV-cache requests and batching-sensitive customers.
- No straightforward way to pre-warm capacity for a new runtime version or to reserve fallback headroom for canary rollouts.

Goals:
1) Implement an Upgrade Wave Controller (UWC) that: orchestrates waves of node/drain/replace with explicit capacity budgets and autoscaler handshake semantics.
2) Add an Autoscaler Handshake API: advertise desired 'reserve' and 'release' intents to the autoscaler to avoid overshoot and ensure headroom during drain.
3) Support LTS channel pinning so customers on an LTS can be scheduled for subset waves and not forced into mixed-version servicing.
4) Provide pre-warm primitives: ability to create warm standby nodes (same model/quantization profile) before draining targets.
5) Expose observability and rollback gates: SLO-based gate checks, request-level tail latency, token/sec throughput, and error rate thresholds.

Proposed design (high level):
- Wave Definition: a wave is a set of target nodes in a GPU pool, an evacuation_budget (percent of pool tokens allowed to be moved), and a prewarm_count.
- Handshake with autoscaler: UWC posts a short-lived ReserveRequest(resource_type=GPU, count=N, ttl=300s). Autoscaler fulfills by provisioning nodes into a prewarm label pool and reports back. Until Reserve fulfilled, UWC stalls draining that would reduce capacity below runway.
- Evacuation budget enforcement: UWC tracks active KV cache occupancy and live inflight request counts; it prevents taking more nodes offline if estimated effective concurrency would breach the evacuation_budget.
- Canary ramp policy: small percentage wave against labeled canary tenants (customers with canary flag or internal traffic); after gate checks, expand waves progressively.
- LTS-aware targeting: when a pool is mixed LTS and non-LTS, UWC will schedule upgrades per LTS cohort to avoid implicit migrations.
- Fallback path: if prewarm nodes fail health checks or SLOs degrade beyond thresholds, UWC aborts and triggers autoscaler release of prewarm capacity, and schedules a rollback to prior model image.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (staging): implement handshake API + simulated UWC in staging with synthetic traffic. Validate reserve/release semantics and timeouts.
- Phase 1 (internal canary): run UWC on 1 dedicated pool with internal-only traffic; enable pre-warm counts and monitor SLOs.
- Phase 2 (customer canary): select low-risk customers and run a single small wave; collect telemetry for 48h.
- Phase 3 (gradual expansion): increase wave sizes up to 20% per window with autoscaler reservations and health gates.

Metrics and gates (examples):
- Gate metrics: 99th percentile latency (generation), error rate (4xx/5xx), model token throughput, prewarm node boot success rate, KV cache hit ratio.
- Rollback criteria: 99p latency increase > 25% sustained for 10m OR error rate increase > 1% absolute over baseline OR prewarm failure rate > 10% for two successive waves.

Implementation tasks (rough breakup):
- UWC controller service + CRD (or config) to describe waves (4 pts)
- Autoscaler handshake API + controller changes to honor ReserveRequest (3 pts)
- Prewarm node lifecycle + health checks (2 pts)
- Evacuation budget estimator using KV occupancy and inflight profiling (3 pts)
- LTS cohorting scheduler and labeling rules (2 pts)
- Observability: dashboards, traces, kpis, and gate plumbing (2 pts)
- E2E integration tests and chaos scenarios (3 pts)

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Autoscaler changes could introduce new scaling regressions. Mitigation: feature-flag the handshake with a dry-run mode that logs but does not affect decisions.
- Risk: Incorrect evacuation estimation may cause customer-visible latency. Mitigation: conservative defaults (small evacuation_budget), staged ramping, and telemetry-based tuning.
- Risk: Prewarm nodes may be stale wrt model image/quantization. Mitigation: artifact promotion & image immutability for prewarm images; prewarm health verification before acceptance.

Dependencies:
- ENG-13011 (node-evacuation-autoscaler-sync) -- rely on its diagnostics and drain lifecycle improvements
- ENG-17488 (orchestrated-canary-fallbacks-for-dedicated-pools) -- we will piggyback on canary policy definitions
- infra/team: boot-time image pipeline and prewarm AMI/container images

Acceptance criteria:
- UWC can reserve capacity and coordinate a 5% wave with no SLO regression for 24h in staging.
- Autoscaler honors ReserveRequest in dry-run and active mode without causing oscillation.
- Observability surfaces prewarm health and gate decisions for all waves.

Deliverables:
- RFC in docs/ (link below) describing handshake API and CRD schema.
- K8s controller implementation and canary deployment.
- Dashboards and alerting for wave progress and rollback triggers.
- Playbook for oncall to intervene and rollback an upgrade wave.
